svg.aria-label: Azure user-defined routes and route tables: the full four-rule selection order with its carve-outs, the default system routes including eight that drop traffic, the side effects of a default route, next hop types and appliance constraints, and route table limits and diagnostics
svg.title: Azure route selection is four rules and a carve-out, not the priority list: longest prefix match runs first, so a user-defined route can lose to a system route nobody wrote
svg.text: UDR beats BGP beats system — and that is the LAST rule Azure checks, not the first
THE FULL SELECTION ORDER
1. LONGEST PREFIX MATCH
specificity wins, whoever wrote the route
a /16 system route beats your /8 user-defined route
2. Explicit prefix over tag
on an exact match, a literal range beats a service tag
3. Service tag hierarchy
regional → top-level → AzureCloud regional → AzureCloud
4. Type priority
UDR → BGP → system — only among EQUAL prefixes
CARVE-OUT: VNet, peering and service-endpoint system routes beat BGP even when BGP is more specific.
EVERY SUBNET STARTS WITH THESE — EIGHT OF THEM DROP TRAFFIC
unique to the VNet
Virtual network
covers subnet-to-subnet; no per-subnet routes exist
Internet
Azure service traffic stays on the backbone
None
RFC 1918 — dropped
None
RFC 6598 — dropped
None
dropped, and NOT explained
Claim a reserved range in your VNet and its None route flips to Virtual network. The drop exists because the range is unused, not forbidden.
ADDING ONE ROUTE DELETES SEVERAL YOU DID NOT WRITE
A 0.0.0.0/0 user-defined route causes the None drop routes to be REMOVED.
Before: traffic to unclaimed RFC 1918 space hits None and is DROPPED at the subnet.
After: the drop routes are gone, so the same traffic matches 0.0.0.0/0 and is FORWARDED to your firewall.
The route you wrote never mentions 10.0.0.0/8. A change meant to tighten control loosened it, in a direction nothing warns about.
Overriding 0.0.0.0/0 also captures AZURE SERVICE traffic, and the subnet stops being directly reachable
from the internet. A service endpoint escapes it — not by overriding, but by being a LONGER prefix.
NEXT HOP TYPES, AND A GATEWAY YOU DO NOT CHOOSE
You CAN specify: Virtual appliance · Virtual network gateway · None · Virtual network · Internet
You CANNOT specify: Virtual network peering · VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint — Azure creates those only.
An appliance in the SAME subnet as its clients loops — the table applies to the appliance too.
Needs Enable IP forwarding in Azure AND possibly in the guest OS. Next hop must be directly connected.
Next hop “Virtual network gateway” works ONLY if the VNet’s gateway is a VPN gateway — and that is an
ELECTION: Route Server wins · else ExpressRoute beats VPN · a Virtual WAN hub always wins.
So adding a Route Server or ExpressRoute gateway silently invalidates working UDRs. Your table did not change.
The election also runs across gateway transit, so a change in the HUB alters every spoke’s routing semantics.
You cannot write a UDR toward an ExpressRoute gateway — that is BGP’s job. Away from it is yours.
TABLES, LIMITS AND THE ONE RELIABLE DIAGNOSTIC
Asymmetric
one table → many subnets, but a subnet holds ZERO OR ONE table. Intents cannot be
composed — they must be merged by hand into a single list.
Limits
400 UDRs per table → 1,000 with Virtual Network Manager (2.5×) · only 25 using service tags
GatewaySubnet
a 0.0.0.0/0 route OR disabled route propagation each stops the gateway working.
Exempt it explicitly from any estate-wide routing policy. Disabling propagation also drops STATIC routes.
Diagnose
effective routes mark the loser Invalid rather than hiding it — the only reliable view.
State is PER SUBNET: the same route can be Invalid for one subnet and Active for another.
A next hop IP of None on a gateway or appliance route means the device may not be running.
Service-endpoint routes cannot be overridden by ANY route table, so enabling one puts that service’s traffic permanently beyond routing-based inspection.
Service tags as route prefixes let Microsoft maintain the addresses for you — the same property that makes them useful in NSGs, applied to routing.
The scale answers are to raise the ceiling (Virtual Network Manager) or remove the competing routes (disablePeeringRoute). Summarising reduces the need for both.
